blocks.text: Just as among birds, too, both the ossifrage and the deep-voiced doves and the races of eagles have a constant love for their offspring. Truly, then, does Jerome say on Isaiah, chapter 66: Those who have written on the nature of animals say that an affection for their offspring and young is inborn in all beasts, beasts of burden, cattle and birds, but that the greatest love is that of eagles. But, what is most to the point, Suidas, under the word Εὔξενος [Euxenos], has this about the eagle's chicks, without naming his author: Οἱ νέοι τῶν ἀετῶν ἐν ἁπαλῷ μὲν τῷ πτερῷ παραπέτονται τοῖς γειναμένοις, μελετώμενοι ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν τὴν πτῆσιν· [Hoi neoi tōn aetōn en hapalō men tō pterō parapetontai tois geinamenois, meletōmenoi hyp᾽ autōn tēn ptēsin] The chicks of eagles, while their feathers are still weak, fly about their parents, learning flight from them. These words are so similar to those of Moses that they could seem to have been copied either from Moses himself or from some translator of Moses. In fact he took them from Philostratus, Apollonius, book 1, chapter 5, where they are read word for word. Yet Philostratus had not read Moses; rather, both described the nature of eagles in this respect. Not unlike this is what Albertus reports he saw: a goshawk, that is, a larger hawk, which threw live birds it had caught to its chicks so that they might pursue, catch and kill them, and thus gradually accustom themselves to hunting. Against this it is objected in vain that Aristotle says the eagle throws its chicks out of the nest when they grow up. Nor is that true without qualification. Rather, out of two or three it throws out one, because it is not able to rear more, just as the ancient Romans exposed those of their children whom they were unable to bring up. The Philosopher himself teaches this, Hist. book 6, ch. 6: Ἐκβάλλει δ᾽ αὐξανομένων τὸν ἕτερον τῶν νεοττῶν, ἀχθόμενος τῇ ἐδωδῇ· [Ekballei d᾽ auxanomenōn ton heteron tōn neottōn, achthomenos tē edōdē] When the chicks grow up, it throws one out, weary of feeding it. For during the time of rearing the mother is often burdened, and almost overwhelmed, by very severe hardships, as follows in the Philosopher: Λέγεται ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ τούτῳ ἄπαστος γίνεσθαι, ὅπως μὴ ἁρπάζῃ τοὺς τῶν θηρίων σκύμνους. οἵ τε οὖν ὄνυχες αὐτοῦ διαστρέφονται ὀλίγας ἡμέρας, καὶ τὰ πτερὰ λευκαίνεται. [Legetai en tō chronō toutō apastos ginesthai, hopōs mē harpazē tous tōn thēriōn skymnous. hoi te oun onyches autou diastrephontai oligas hēmeras, kai ta ptera leukainetai.] Pliny imitates this as follows: For at that time nature has denied them food, taking care that the young of all wild beasts should not be carried off. Their talons too are turned back during those days, and their feathers turn white from want of food. If, then, in these straits the mother throws out one of the chicks, she is forced to it by sheer necessity, as when for fear of shipwreck the cargo is thrown into [II, 766] the sea, as in Ion. I, 5. and Act. XXVII, 19. Ambrose, in the place cited above, gives another answer: namely, that the eagle casts out only those which, when exposed to the rays of the sun, turn their eyes away as degenerate; and so it becomes harsh not from stinginess in feeding but from the test of judgment; nor does it, as it were, disown its own chick when it expels it from the nest, but rejects it as a stranger's.
